units.subject: Civic Education
units.title: Citizenship Education
objectives: Explain the central ideas in this source topic and relate them to responsible citizenship.
Apply the topic to realistic civic situations and answer structured examination questions.
units.body: Citizenship education develops the knowledge, values and practical skills people need to participate responsibly in public life. It helps learners understand citizenship, how public institutions operate, how rights are protected, and why duties such as obeying lawful rules and respecting other people matter. It is not simply memorising government facts: students should apply civic principles to everyday decisions at home, school and in the wider community. A citizen is a person recognised by a state as belonging to it under that state's law. Citizenship may be acquired through routes recognised by the constitution and legislation, such as birth, registration or naturalisation, subject to applicable conditions. Citizenship is distinct from residence: a person may live in a country without being its citizen. Citizenship education supports peaceful coexistence by teaching respect for diversity, constitutional values, tolerance, accountability and informed participation. Rights and responsibilities should be taught together: exercising a right does not permit a person to violate another person's rights.

units.subject: Civic Education
units.title: Duties and Obligations of Citizens
objectives: Explain the central ideas in this source topic and relate them to responsible citizenship.
Apply the topic to realistic civic situations and answer structured examination questions.
units.body: A duty or obligation is a responsibility a person is expected or legally required to perform. Citizens' obligations help a society function fairly and safely. They include obeying valid laws, respecting the rights of others, paying taxes when legally liable, participating in elections when eligible, protecting public property, and contributing to community life. Civic duties are often grouped into political, economic and social responsibilities. Political responsibilities include informed voting by eligible citizens, lawful participation in public affairs and respect for constitutional institutions. Economic responsibilities include paying taxes and complying with lawful financial obligations. Social responsibilities include respecting others, protecting public facilities, assisting community initiatives and promoting peaceful relations. Age and legal capacity matter. A student below voting age is not expected to vote, but can still learn about public issues, respect others' rights and contribute to school or community activities. Duties must be carried out lawfully: citizens do not acquire general police powers merely because they have a responsibility to support public safety.

units.subject: Civic Education
units.title: Promotion of Our Traditions and Customs
objectives: Explain the central ideas in this source topic and relate them to responsible citizenship.
Apply the topic to realistic civic situations and answer structured examination questions.
units.body: Customs are shared practices and accepted ways of behaving within a community. Traditions are beliefs, ceremonies, knowledge and practices transmitted across generations. They may include language, music, dance, dress, food, crafts, festivals, oral history and forms of community organisation. Cultural heritage contributes to identity and can help people understand their history and maintain social bonds. It can be promoted through teaching local languages, documenting oral histories, supporting museums and cultural centres, encouraging responsible festivals, preserving traditional arts and crafts, and including accurate cultural studies in education. Families and community elders can pass on knowledge, while schools, media and public institutions can create opportunities for different communities to share their heritage respectfully. Nigeria is culturally diverse. Promotion of one community's heritage should not imply that other groups are inferior or that every person from a group follows the same practice. Cultural practices also need to be assessed against constitutional rights, dignity, equality and safety.

units.subject: Civic Education
units.title: National Consciousness, Integrity and Unity
objectives: Explain the central ideas in this source topic and relate them to responsible citizenship.
Apply the topic to realistic civic situations and answer structured examination questions.
units.body: National consciousness is awareness of belonging to a country and an informed concern for its wellbeing. It involves understanding national symbols, history, institutions, constitutional principles and shared responsibilities. National unity is the willingness of people from different communities to live and work together as members of one political society while respecting their differences. Integrity means acting honestly and consistently with sound ethical principles, including when there is no immediate reward. In public life, integrity requires truthful communication, fair treatment, responsible use of public resources and refusal to abuse entrusted authority. Unity is not the absence of disagreement; citizens can debate policies while remaining committed to lawful and peaceful ways of resolving differences. National consciousness can be strengthened by civic education, inclusive public institutions, respect for the constitution, fair access to opportunity, responsible leadership, inter-community cooperation and accurate knowledge of national history.

units.subject: Civic Education
units.title: Capitalist Democracy
objectives: Explain the central ideas in this source topic and relate them to responsible citizenship.
Apply the topic to realistic civic situations and answer structured examination questions.
units.body: Democracy is a system of government in which public authority is derived from the people and exercised through constitutional institutions. In a representative democracy, citizens choose representatives through periodic elections. Essential features include political participation, genuine electoral choice, the rule of law, protection of fundamental rights, accountability, public debate and peaceful transfer of power. Capitalism is an economic system in which productive assets may be privately owned and economic activity is substantially organised through markets, investment and exchange. A capitalist democracy combines democratic political institutions with an economy in which private enterprise and market activity play a major role. The political and economic systems are related but not identical: holding elections does not automatically guarantee fair economic opportunity, and private ownership does not itself guarantee democratic government. A democratic state sets legal rules for economic activity, protects lawful property rights, regulates markets where necessary and remains responsible for public goods and social protection.

units.subject: Civic Education
units.title: Political Party
objectives: Explain the central ideas in this source topic and relate them to responsible citizenship.
Apply the topic to realistic civic situations and answer structured examination questions.
units.body: A political party is an organised association of people who share broad political goals and seek to influence or control government through constitutional political processes, especially elections. Parties develop policy programmes, select or support candidates, campaign, mobilise voters and organise elected representatives. They connect citizens' concerns with public decision-making. Political parties differ from pressure groups. A party normally seeks elected office and responsibility for governing, while a pressure group seeks to influence policy without necessarily contesting elections to form a government. Civil society organisations may monitor public institutions, provide services or advocate for causes; they are not automatically political parties. In a democratic system, parties can present alternative programmes, recruit leaders, educate voters, aggregate interests and provide opposition scrutiny. Healthy party competition requires internal organisation, transparent candidate selection, lawful campaign finance, peaceful conduct and respect for electoral outcomes.

units.subject: Civic Education
units.title: Poverty and Its Effects
objectives: Explain the central ideas in this source topic and relate them to responsible citizenship.
Apply the topic to realistic civic situations and answer structured examination questions.
units.body: Poverty is a condition in which people lack sufficient resources to meet essential needs and participate adequately in society. It may involve inadequate income, food insecurity, unsafe housing, limited access to education and healthcare, insecure work or exclusion from essential services. Poverty is multidimensional: two households with similar income may face different levels of hardship because of health, location, household size or access to public services. Poverty can contribute to malnutrition, preventable illness, interrupted schooling, unsafe living conditions and reduced opportunities. It can increase vulnerability to exploitation and make it harder for people to participate in community and political life. These effects are shaped by employment opportunities, public infrastructure, economic conditions, education, health and social protection. Responses include access to quality education, decent work, skills development, reliable infrastructure, effective public services, fair economic opportunities and targeted support for vulnerable households.

units.subject: Civic Education
units.title: Political Apathy
objectives: Explain the central ideas in this source topic and relate them to responsible citizenship.
Apply the topic to realistic civic situations and answer structured examination questions.
units.body: Political apathy is a lack of interest in or willingness to participate in political processes. It may appear as failure to register where eligible, refusal to vote, avoidance of public discussion or disengagement from civic organisations. It should not be confused with lawful criticism: a citizen who questions a candidate or rejects a policy is still engaging with public affairs. Factors associated with political apathy can include distrust caused by unfulfilled promises, perceived electoral malpractice, political violence, intimidation, lack of accessible information, poverty, exclusion and the belief that participation will not make a difference. Some people face practical barriers such as disability access, distance from polling facilities or work obligations. Measures to reduce apathy include credible and impartial election administration, accessible civic education, transparent public decisions, safe participation, accountability for misconduct, inclusive consultation and peaceful political competition.

units.subject: Civic Education
units.title: Why Leaders Fail to Protect the Interest of Their Followers
objectives: Explain the central ideas in this source topic and relate them to responsible citizenship.
Apply the topic to realistic civic situations and answer structured examination questions.
units.body: Leaders are entrusted with authority to make decisions and act on behalf of a group or community. They fail to protect followers' interests when they place personal advantage, private networks or party interests above public responsibilities. Other contributing factors may include weak institutions, poor access to information, lack of transparency, conflicts of interest, intimidation of critics and ineffective oversight. Good leadership requires honesty, competence, fairness, consultation, respect for rights and willingness to explain decisions. Leaders should use public resources for authorised purposes, disclose relevant conflicts, listen to affected communities and apply rules consistently. Accountability can be strengthened through independent oversight, transparent budgets, credible elections, access to public information, legislative scrutiny, judicial review and lawful complaint mechanisms. These safeguards do not guarantee perfect leadership, but they make abuse more difficult to conceal and easier to challenge.
